t0496c8db: The average European household does 3–5 wash loads per week. In this worksheet you will investigate how much energy and water a washing machine uses on different programmes, compare types of tumble dryer, and calculate what you could save by choosing eco settings.
t26eae0a9: A **washing machine** is one of the biggest water and electricity users in a home. Most of the energy goes into **heating water** – not spinning the drum. Modern washing machines include **eco modes** that use less water and lower temperatures, though they often take longer to run.
t5fc17b37: Heating water to 40°C or 60°C uses far more energy than running the motor. An Eco program at 20°C – 30°C uses **up to 60% less energy** but runs longer.
t8b8de1a1: **The trade-off:** longer cycle time but lower cost and less fabric damage.
t35abccf6: **Clothe dryers** are even more energy intensive. Understanding the difference between **vented** and **condenser** dryers – and when to avoid using a dryer at all – can save money and reduce emissions.
t8ed87545: **Vented dryer:** Pulls in room air, heats it, blows humid air out through a hose (must be vented outside). High energy use (typical: 2.5–3.5 kWh per load).
tb933dcab: **Condenser dryer:** No vent needed. Moisture is collected in a tank. Slightly more efficient (2.0–3.0 kWh per load) but slower.
te0d5a492: **Heat pump dryer:** Most efficient (1.0–1.5 kWh per load) – uses a refrigerant cycle like a fridge. It is more expensive to buy but cheaper to run.
tc435ac92: **Water use:** Washing machines typically use 40–90 litres per cycle, depending on drum size and programme. Eco programmes tend to use less water because they spin more slowly and re-use rinse water more efficiently.
tbc971ada: Energy to heat water = $\text{liters}\times 4.18\times ΔT/3600$ kWh (simplified: ~0.05 kWh per litre per 10°C temperature rise).
